findings.title: hardcoded-secrets check flat-critical across ~30 secret patterns, double-counts Google keys
findings.summary: Walmart scan: Google API keys matched by generic hardcoded-secrets (severity critical) pushed the whole scan to unsafe/10, despite two dedicated checks (google-api-key-exposed, secret-google-maps-api-key) already correctly rating the same evidence as medium. Client-exposed-by-design keys (Google/Firebase) should not carry the same severity as server-only secrets (AWS/Stripe/DB URIs).
findings.fix: Split hardcoded-secrets into 4 severity-tiered check ids (hardcoded-secrets critical / hardcoded-secrets-high-risk high / hardcoded-secrets-client-exposed medium / hardcoded-secrets-low-risk low) in lib/scanner/checks/code.ts + checks-data/code.json. Removed the Google API Key (AIzaSy*) pattern entirely -- google-api-key-exposed (content.json) and secret-google-maps-api-key/secret-firebase-api-key-public (secrets-extended.json) already cover that evidence at medium/low. Also fixed safety-rating.ts's dead 'Hardcoded API Keys' exploitablePatterns entry (never matched any real title) so the new tiers classify as exploitable-at-their-own-severity instead of falling into 'hardening' or being dropped -- merged with scanner-02's independent fix for the same dead pattern (broader regex, kept as-is). Shipped by agent a9eefbf8ba0b78d5c.

findings.title: Danger score / safety rating ignore AI verification verdicts entirely
findings.summary: getSafetyRating/getDangerScore in lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts weight every finding by severity+title pattern only; a finding the AI already flagged possible_fp counts at full weight, defeating the verification pipeline. Confirmed on Walmart scan: several cookie findings marked possible_fp (detector cited a cookie not present in the live probe) still counted at full weight toward the unsafe/10 verdict.
findings.fix: Extend Finding interface with aiVerdict/aiConfidence, weight accordingly. In progress (agent adf62015a31287147).

findings.title: checkSecurityTxt probes bare apex host, misses www-only security.txt
findings.summary: Walmart scan reported security.txt missing at both well-known/root paths on walmart.com; user manually confirmed www.walmart.com serves a valid security.txt. Apex/www host mismatch in lib/scanner/async-checks.ts's checkSecurityTxt, likely a redirect-handling or origin-source bug.
findings.fix: Root-causing redirect/origin handling. In progress (agent a4a7418e77b0d7ded).

findings.title: AI verification timeout/chunk-size too tight for realistic finding counts
findings.summary: lib/ai/verify-findings.ts's verifyInChunks stops at a 90s total deadline with chunk size 5; only ~35-40 of Walmart's 57 findings received an AI verdict before the deadline hit, the rest silently unverified with no coverage indicator.
findings.fix: Increasing CONFIG_AI_VERIFY_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS/CHUNK_SIZE with worst-case arithmetic, checking client-side timeout parity. In progress (agent a567911127be41393).

findings.title: Discord sign-in/sign-up redirect URI never documented for registration
findings.summary: The unified sign-in/sign-up OAuth flow added in app/api/v3/auth/oauth/[provider]/ redirects to /api/v3/auth/oauth/discord/callback for Discord, a distinct URI from the older Profile > Connections linking flow's /api/v3/auth/discord/callback. .env.example (and the operator's own .env.local) only ever documented the older URI for the Discord Developer Portal. A self-hoster (or this SaaS's own Discord app, if registered before the unified flow existed) who followed that doc registers only one of the two required redirect URIs, so the Sign in with Discord / Sign up with Discord buttons on /login and /signup -- which render whenever DISCORD_CLIENT_ID/SECRET are set, per /api/v3/auth/oauth/info -- fail at Discord with a redirect_uri mismatch, while the Profile Connect button keeps working. Same bug class as cc1b1f9f's GitHub repo-connect fix earlier today, but Discord's two flows are intentionally separate (not merged), so the fix is registering both URIs rather than consolidating callbacks.
findings.fix: Documented both required OAuth2 redirect URLs in the Discord Developer Portal section of .env.example -- confirm the production/sandbox Discord app also has both registered.

findings.title: content.json metadata copy-paste drift: 4 checks show completely wrong title/description/evidence
findings.summary: form-action-tel-scheme, sourcemap-reference, discord-webhook-exposed, and exposed-session-id in content.json each had title/description/evidence/riskImpact/fixSteps text belonging to a DIFFERENT check (e.g. form-action-tel-scheme's JSON said 'Forms Submitting to External Domains' while its detector actually checks for tel: scheme form actions; sourcemap-reference's JSON was entirely about cookie max-age; discord-webhook-exposed's JSON was entirely about WordPress admin paths; exposed-session-id's JSON was about missing cookie flags while the detector actually checks for a session ID in the URL). Real scan findings showed users a title/description unrelated to the actual evidence.
findings.fix: Rewrote all 4 JSON entries' title/description/evidence/riskImpact/explanation/fixSteps/codeExamples to match what their detector functions actually check; corrected severities (tel-scheme medium->low, discord-webhook low->medium) and the 'type' field (sourcemap-reference/exposed-session-id combined|header-value -> body-pattern, fixing an inflated engine-confidence score for a body-regex check).

findings.title: service-worker-scope always fires at high severity on ordinary PWA service worker registration
findings.summary: The detector regex captured only the URL string argument of navigator.serviceWorker.register(...), never the options object, so it could never see an explicit scope option -- meaning the 'broad scope' condition was true for virtually every register() call including ones that DO narrow scope. Combined with a JSON title/description claiming 'Registered Over Insecure HTTP' (unrelated to what the code checks) at severity high, this fired at high severity on the single most common, expected PWA pattern (navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')) -- the same class of bug as the Walmart incident (standard pattern flagged as if dangerous).
findings.fix: Fixed the regex to capture the full register(...) call so a real scope option is actually visible; corrected the JSON title/description/evidence to describe broad-scope detection instead of HTTP insecurity; downgraded severity high -> low since broad scope is the expected default for most PWAs, not itself exploitable.

findings.title: graphql-introspection titled 'Enabled in Production' but only detects a string reference in the client bundle
findings.summary: Detector matches __schema{/IntrospectionQuery/getIntrospectionQuery anywhere in body -- text bundled by nearly every GraphQL client library (Apollo, Relay, graphql-request) for fragment matching/codegen, regardless of whether the server's introspection is actually enabled. The JSON title asserted introspection is 'Enabled in Production' (a claim about live server behavior the check never verifies), at medium severity, so any GraphQL-using site (common at Walmart scale) would false-positive on ordinary client tooling.
findings.fix: Retitled to 'GraphQL Introspection Query Reference Found', rewrote description/riskImpact/fixSteps to say this is a client-bundle reference requiring separate server-side verification, and downgraded severity medium -> low.

findings.title: bearer-token-exposed regex matches API-doc placeholder tokens, rated critical
findings.summary: The regex /Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9._\-+\/=]{20,}/i matches the extremely common documentation placeholder style 'Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN_HERE' / 'Bearer API_KEY_PLACEHOLDER' (all-caps-with-underscores is never a real base64/JWT token), yet was rated critical -- the same severity class as a confirmed hardcoded database credential -- and higher than the near-identical jwt-in-html check (rated high) in the same file.
findings.fix: Excluded all-caps/underscore-only matches from firing (placeholder convention, never a real secret) and downgraded severity critical -> high to match jwt-in-html's precedent for the same evidence class.

findings.title: sensitive-form-no-csrf fires on forms that submit to a third-party domain
findings.summary: Any POST form was flagged for missing a CSRF token field even when its action attribute pointed to a different origin entirely (e.g. a Mailchimp/HubSpot-hosted newsletter signup form). A form that never reaches your own backend cannot be protected by your CSRF tokens -- that's the third party's concern, not a gap in your app -- so this fired constantly on ordinary marketing pages with embedded third-party forms, on top of double-counting evidence already covered by the separate open-form-action check.
findings.fix: Skip forms whose action attribute is an absolute cross-origin URL before evaluating for a missing CSRF field; same-origin/relative-action forms are still checked as before.

findings.title: debug-endpoint rated high while the near-identical sensitive-endpoints check is rated low
findings.summary: Both checks fire on the same evidence class -- an unverified path-fragment string (e.g. '/debug/', '/trace/') appearing anywhere in the page body, with no confirmation the endpoint is reachable or that the string isn't from an observability/tracing vendor's own URLs (Datadog, OpenTelemetry, etc. commonly reference '/trace/' paths in their own tags). debug-endpoint was rated high, four tiers above the equivalent-strength sensitive-endpoints check (low), for the same 'found a suspicious substring in a huge page/JS bundle' evidence pattern the audit is specifically targeting.
findings.fix: Downgraded debug-endpoint severity high -> low for parity with sensitive-endpoints.

findings.title: iframe-srcdoc-no-sandbox mistyped as 'header' (93% confidence) and described as generic third-party src widgets
findings.summary: The JSON 'type' field controls the engine-confidence score assigned to a finding (header=93%, body-pattern=70% per registry.ts); this check's detector is a pure body regex on iframe srcdoc attributes but was typed 'header', overstating confidence for one of the more FP-prone categories. Its description also talked about 'third-party widgets (Stripe, YouTube)' loaded without sandbox, which describes src= iframes, not the srcdoc= iframes this specific check actually inspects -- confusing overlap with the separate iframe-sandbox-missing check.
findings.fix: Corrected type header -> body-pattern and rewrote the description/riskImpact to describe srcdoc-specific inline-HTML risk instead of generic third-party embeds.

findings.title: vibe-code category self-triggers on any page documenting its own example patterns, including this product's own /docs pages
findings.summary: None of vibe-code.ts's 31 detectors scoped their regex search to actual <script> content -- they scan the full page body/text. Every detector's 'bad' example (eval(), SQL string concatenation, hardcoded password comparisons, JWT none-alg, etc.) is exactly the kind of snippet a tutorial, security blog, or API-documentation page renders as literal text inside <pre>/<code> blocks for teaching purposes. This product's own /docs/api page renders every check's codeExamples field (including the 'Bad (AI-generated)' samples) as literal HTML text, so scanning VulnRadar's own docs would self-trigger a large fraction of this entire category -- the same 'no context requirement, matches on huge blocks of unrelated/informational text' failure mode called out for this audit, just self-inflicted.
findings.fix: Added a new stripDocBlocks() helper (lib/scanner/_helpers.ts) that removes <code>/<pre>/<kbd>/<samp> regions but NOT <script> tags (several detectors need real script content), and wrapped every vibe-code detector to run against the stripped body.

findings.title: vibe-http-not-https fires on every page with an inline SVG or JSON-LD structured-data block
findings.summary: The hardcoded-http-url regex excluded localhost/127.0.0.1/example.com but not the http:// XML/RDF namespace and vocabulary URIs that are spec identifiers, never network requests: xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" (present on virtually every site with an inline SVG icon) and "@context":"http://schema.org" (present on virtually every SEO-conscious site's JSON-LD product/article markup -- this project's own recent SEO commit added exactly this). Both would false-positive as a 'Hardcoded HTTP URL' finding.
findings.fix: Added www.w3.org, schema.org, ogp.me, purl.org, and creativecommons.org to the exclusion list.

findings.title: vibe-loose-equality-auth rated high but scans client-delivered JS, where the pattern is almost always harmless UI-gating
findings.summary: This check is a body-pattern scan of the page's own delivered scripts, not server source. 'role == "admin"' or similar in a browser bundle is overwhelmingly ordinary client-side conditional rendering (show/hide an admin link) driven by a value the server already decided was safe to send -- not the actual authorization boundary, which lives server-side and is never visible in the response body being scanned. Rating this high implies a near-certain auth bypass; in practice it is nearly always benign UI code.
findings.fix: Downgraded severity high -> low and added a caveat to the description clarifying the client-side context and that this should prompt checking the real backend logic, not be read as confirmation of a bypass.

findings.title: Three cookie fingerprint checks titled 'missing security attributes' only ever checked the cookie NAME, never the attributes
findings.summary: django-csrftoken-cookie-exposed, laravel-session-cookie-exposes, and express-cookie-exposes all had a JSON title/description claiming to detect a session/CSRF cookie 'missing security attributes' (Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite), at medium severity -- but the detector bodies only matched the framework's DEFAULT cookie name (csrftoken, XSRF-TOKEN, connect.sid, etc.) and returned a finding unconditionally, never inspecting the cookie string for the attributes the title claims are missing. A site using the default cookie name with fully correct Secure+HttpOnly+SameSite flags set would still get flagged as if attributes were absent. (The sibling rails-cookie-httponly check in the same file does this correctly, which is how the gap was found.)
findings.fix: Rewrote all three detectors to actually check for missing Secure/SameSite/HttpOnly on the matched cookie (correctly NOT requiring HttpOnly on Django's csrftoken / Laravel's XSRF-TOKEN, which are intentionally JS-readable by design) and only fire when an attribute is genuinely absent.

findings.title: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: open-form-action's third-party allowlist (stripe/paypal/google only) is likely too narrow for real-world marketing pages
findings.summary: The check flags any POST form whose action points to an external domain not in {stripe.com, paypal.com, google.com}, at medium severity. Large real-world sites commonly embed newsletter/contact forms hosted by Mailchimp (*.list-manage.com), HubSpot (hsforms.com), Typeform, Formspree, SurveyMonkey, etc., none of which are allowlisted -- plausible to false-positive on an ordinary marketing site. Left unfixed because deciding which third parties are 'legitimate enough' to allowlist is a product/policy call, not a pure bug fix, and an incomplete allowlist just moves the false-positive boundary rather than eliminating it.

findings.title: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: content.ts's postmessage-origin and client-side.ts's postmessage-no-origin-check are near-duplicate detectors
findings.summary: Both fire on the identical evidence: any addEventListener('message', ...) in the page with no '.origin' usage anywhere in body, both at severity high. A page with an unvalidated postMessage listener produces TWO separate high-severity findings under two different check IDs (content and client-side categories) for one real signal, double-counting it in the danger score. Left unfixed because the right resolution -- retire one, or make them meaningfully distinct (e.g. one requires a nearby dangerous sink) -- is a design decision about which category should own postMessage-origin detection, not a pure bug fix, and I did not want to unilaterally deprecate a check ID that other code/AI-verification logic might reference.

findings.title: Duplicate header checks double-count the same evidence at inconsistent severities
findings.summary: Seven pairs of header detectors fire on the exact same underlying condition under different ids/severities: csp-frame-ancestors is a strict subset of clickjack-missing; x-content-type-options-not-nosniff duplicates nosniff-incorrect (and its own JSON metadata described the wrong 'missing header' scenario, not what it actually detected); corp-missing duplicates cross-origin-resource-policy-report-only-missing; server-timing-sensitive-key-leak duplicates server-timing-exposure and its keyword list flagged the benign, extremely common 'cache;dur=NN' CDN timing value as 'sensitive'; x-frame-options-invalid re-fired on XFO:ALLOWALL despite x-frame-options-allowall already covering it at higher severity; hsts-no-preload double-reported 'missing includeSubDomains' alongside the dedicated strict-transport-security-include-subdomains check; referrer-policy-no-referrer-strict-origin-when-cross-origin double-reported 'unsafe-url'/'no-referrer-when-downgrade' alongside referrer-policy-unsafe. Each pair inflated finding counts and danger-score contributions for one real signal.
findings.fix: Disabled the redundant/subset detector in each pair (return null with an explanatory comment, matching the file's existing etag-inode-leak convention) or narrowed the broader detector's condition to stop overlapping with the more precise one.

findings.title: Stale/renamed header check ids left title+description describing an unrelated concept
findings.summary: coop-missing, corp-missing (before scanner-05's dedup), charset-meta-missing, and cors-null-origin-allowed all had their real detector logic implemented under an id that used to represent something else entirely: coop-missing's title/description talk about the optional Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy-Report-Only preview variant while the code checks the real enforcing COOP header; charset-meta-missing's metadata was entirely about 'Sec-Fetch-* Request Headers Not Echoed' while the code checks for a missing <meta charset> tag; cors-null-origin-allowed's metadata was entirely about 'COOP unsafe-popups' while the code detects Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null (a real, moderately serious CORS bypass vector exploitable via sandboxed iframes), and was consequently mis-tiered at severity info. The templated 'evidence' field in each JSON entry still contained the original id slug (e.g. headers-coop-report-only-missing, headers-sec-fetch-missing, headers-coop-same-origin-allow-popups), confirming these ids were repointed to existing detectors without updating the rest of the metadata. Users saw a title/description/fix-steps completely unrelated to what was actually found.
findings.fix: Rewrote title/description/riskImpact/explanation/fixSteps for coop-missing, charset-meta-missing, and cors-null-origin-allowed to match their real detector behavior; bumped cors-null-origin-allowed from info to medium to reflect the real risk (ACAO: null trusted by sandboxed-iframe/data-URI attackers).

findings.title: Several header checks rated medium/high fire on completely standard practice at well-run sites
findings.summary: sri-missing (high) fires on any external script lacking a Subresource Integrity hash, but SRI is fundamentally impractical for continuously-updated third-party vendor scripts (analytics, ads, payment SDKs) that essentially every major site loads, including security-conscious ones -- so this fired at 'high' severity against nearly the entire web. target-blank-no-noopener (medium) flags <a target=_blank> without rel=noopener even though the check's own riskImpact text already concedes Chrome 88+/Firefox 79+ apply noopener behavior by default, making the real-world risk on modern browsers low. iframe-third-party-without-sandbox (medium) fires on any cross-origin iframe including routine, legitimate embeds (YouTube, Google Maps, payment SDKs, chat widgets) that omit sandbox because it would break required functionality, and its own riskImpact overstated the threat (claimed DOM access the Same-Origin Policy already blocks regardless of sandbox). x-backend-server-exposed (medium) fires on X-Served-By, a default Fastly/Varnish header used by many large, well-run sites, at a higher severity than the identical-risk sibling checks (server-header-disclosure, via-header-exposed, x-powered-by-exposed) which are all 'low'.
findings.fix: Lowered sri-missing, target-blank-no-noopener, iframe-third-party-without-sandbox, and x-backend-server-exposed to severity low (matching sibling checks of equivalent real-world risk); corrected iframe-third-party-without-sandbox's explanation to not claim sandbox gates parent-DOM access.

findings.title: Cookie 'third-party' checks conflate having a Domain= attribute with being cross-site
findings.summary: cookie-no-samesite-third-party, cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure, and cookie-partitioned-missing all treated any cookie carrying an explicit Domain= attribute as a 'third-party'/'cross-site' cookie. An explicit Domain attribute is the standard, completely ordinary way to share a session cookie across subdomains for first-party SSO (Domain=example.com set by www.example.com so api.example.com can read it) at any company with multiple subdomains -- it cannot be determined to be cross-site from a single response at all. cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure (high severity) consequently fired on ordinary Domain-scoped cookies using SameSite=Lax/Strict -- a secure, correct configuration -- and told developers to add SameSite=None instead, which is worse remediation advice, not better (it would widen CSRF exposure). cookie-no-samesite-third-party was additionally a strict-subset duplicate of cookie-third-party-no-samesite-none-secure's firing condition.
findings.fix: Disabled all three detectors (return null with an explanatory comment). The precise, correct version of this check already exists and doesn't depend on guessing 'third-party' from Domain=: set-cookie-samesite-none-no-secure fires only when SameSite=None is already explicitly declared but Secure is missing.

findings.title: cookie-domain-broad severity inconsistent with its own sibling check's documented rationale
findings.summary: cookie-domain-broad (medium) fires on Domain=.example.com (leading dot) while cookie-domain-no-leading-dot (low) fires on Domain=example.com (no leading dot). cookie-domain-no-leading-dot's own description already states 'RFC 6265bis deprecates the leading dot, and modern browsers treat both forms identically' -- per RFC 6265 Sec 5.2.3 the leading dot is stripped on receipt and has zero effect, so both forms are equally subdomain-wide with identical real-world risk, yet one was scored 2 tiers higher than the other for the same effective exposure. A broad cookie domain is also completely standard, intentional practice at any company with subdomain-wide SSO.
findings.fix: Lowered cookie-domain-broad from medium to low to match cookie-domain-no-leading-dot, and noted the RFC 6265 rationale directly in its description.

findings.title: ratelimit-policy-missing only checks the newest unprefixed header name, missing the still-common legacy convention its own description promises
findings.summary: The JSON description explicitly says the check looks for 'X-RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Limit, Retry-After', but the detector code only ever checked the new, least-adopted IETF-draft 'RateLimit-Limit' (unprefixed). APIs using the still extremely common legacy X-RateLimit-* convention (GitHub, Twitter/X, and many other well-run APIs) or that only emit Retry-After on throttled responses were false-flagged at medium severity as having 'no RateLimit-* family headers' even though they do rate-limit and do expose it.
findings.fix: Added checks for the legacy x-ratelimit-limit header and retry-after, matching what the description already claimed.

findings.title: content-disposition-inline's isBinary regex matched images/audio/video, firing 'force a download' advice on essentially every image on every site
findings.summary: The 'no Content-Disposition header on binary response' branch used an isBinary regex that, in addition to genuinely downloadable types (PDF, ZIP, DOC, octet-stream, executables), also matched image/*, audio/*, and video/*. Images and video are *supposed* to render inline via /
findings.fix: Narrowed the isBinary check used for the 'missing header' branch to only genuinely downloadable document/archive/executable MIME types, matching what the JSON description already promised.

findings.title: x-xss-protection-block reported a finding for the correct, recommended configuration
findings.summary: A second branch returned a non-null evidence string -- creating an actual finding entry -- whenever an HTML page correctly omitted the deprecated X-XSS-Protection header, with evidence text that literally read '...that's correct (deprecated); ensure CSP is the actual defense.' Omitting a deprecated, no-longer-supported header is the current best practice recommended by MDN/OWASP, not something to flag. Because this fired on every single HTML page of every site that does the right thing, it was likely one of the single largest volume contributors to inflated finding counts of any check reviewed in this sweep.
findings.fix: Removed the branch entirely; the detector now only fires on the genuinely bad state (X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block explicitly set), matching what the JSON title/description already described.

findings.title: secrets-extended.ts's ~51 per-provider secret-* detectors had zero placeholder filtering
findings.summary: Unlike the main hardcoded-secrets detector (which filters matched values against example/your_/xxxx/0000/placeholder/test_/dummy/localhost), none of the per-provider secret-* detectors (secret-stripe-webhook-endpoint, secret-google-maps-api-key, secret-aws-secret-key, etc.) called stripExampleContent or filtered matched values at all. A .env.example served raw, or a README documenting a fake-but-correctly-shaped credential (STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_YOUR_KEY_HERE, AIzaSyXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX), would satisfy a provider's format regex and get reported as a confirmed secret, several at critical severity.
findings.fix: Added maskPlaceholderSecrets() (mirrors hardcoded-secrets' existing exclusion terms) plus stripExampleContent, applied via an export-time wrapper (same pattern as vibe-code.ts's stripDocBlocks wrapper) so every detector receives body with placeholder-marked tokens and doc/example HTML regions already neutralized before its format regex runs. Also fixed secret-auth0-client-secret, which fired on the bare phrase auth0_client_secret with no captured value at all, to require an assignment+value shape.

findings.title: secrets-extended.json's per-provider checks all typed 'header', overstating confidence to 93% for pure body regex
findings.summary: All 51 entries in secrets-extended.json declared type 'header' even though every one of their detectors (confirmed by reading the full .ts file) only examines the response body, never headers. Per registry.ts's confidenceForType, 'header' maps to 93% confidence (near-certain) while the correct 'body-pattern' type maps to 70% -- the same mislabeling class already fixed once for a single content.json check (AUDIT-008 content-07) but present here across an entire file.
findings.fix: Bulk-corrected type: 'header' -> 'body-pattern' for all 51 entries in secrets-extended.json.

findings.title: ssl.ts's mixed-protocol-content had no HTTPS gate, fired 'HTTPS page loading HTTP resources' on plain HTTP pages
findings.summary: detectMixedContent() matched src/href/action="http://..." anywhere in the body with no check that the scanned page itself was HTTPS. Mixed content is only a meaningful concept on an HTTPS page loading HTTP subresources -- an http:// page referencing other http:// URLs (including ordinary same-origin links) is completely normal. This fired on virtually every plain-HTTP page scanned, misreporting them as HTTPS pages with mixed content. The newer PageCheck-architecture equivalents (page-mixed-content-active/passive in page-checks/mixed-content.ts) already correctly gate on ctx.isHttps -- this older detector was the one left behind.
findings.fix: Added an explicit url.startsWith('https://') gate before the mixed-content regex runs.

findings.title: api-rest-mass-assignment-risk (high) inferred an input-validation bug from response content alone
findings.summary: The detector only checks whether a RESPONSE body contains "role":"admin" or "isAdmin":true, then reports it as a mass-assignment vulnerability at high severity with evidence claiming the endpoint 'appears to accept and bind arbitrary request body fields without filtering.' Mass assignment is about what an endpoint accepts as INPUT; a normal /api/me correctly returning the current (legitimately admin) user's own role in a read response satisfies this regex with zero relation to any actual vulnerability, and would fire on any authenticated admin session.
findings.fix: Downgraded high -> low, retitled to 'REST endpoint response exposes privileged fields', and reworded description/evidence to state what was actually observed (privileged field names present in a response) rather than asserting a confirmed mass-assignment vulnerability; also corrected its JSON type from 'header' to 'body-pattern' (the detector never reads headers).

findings.title: api-graphql-suggestions-enabled matched the ubiquitous UI phrase 'did you mean' on any page, unrelated to GraphQL
findings.summary: The regex matched a literal 'did you mean' or 'didYouMean' anywhere in the body with no requirement that the response actually came from a GraphQL endpoint. 'Did you mean' is an extremely common e-commerce/docs search-UI phrase (Google, Amazon-style typo suggestions) with nothing to do with GraphQL schema enumeration, yet the evidence text confidently asserted 'GraphQL error response ... confirming field suggestions are enabled.'
findings.fix: Gated on GraphQL context (/graphql URL or a JSON 'errors' array present) AND required the graphql-js suggestion message shape ('did you mean "fieldName"') that generic UI copy does not replicate.

findings.title: api-graphql-introspection-enabled had an unscoped fallback branch matching any page, same bug class already fixed for content.json's graphql-introspection
findings.summary: A second branch matched ["']__schema["']\s*\{ anywhere in the body with no URL/endpoint scoping at all -- __schema{ is text bundled by Apollo/Relay/graphql-request client libraries for their own fragment matching, present regardless of whether the server's introspection is enabled. This is the identical false-positive pattern already fixed for content.json's graphql-introspection check (AUDIT-008 content-03), just under a different check id in api.json, still at severity high and additionally overclaiming 'returned a full schema dump' with no verification a dump occurred.
findings.fix: Removed the unscoped branch; the remaining branch requires the URL to actually be /graphql AND the body to reference schema/introspection keywords. Downgraded high -> medium and reworded evidence to prompt verification rather than assert the dump occurred; corrected type 'header' -> 'combined' (checks url and body, never headers).

findings.title: idor-sequential-id-in-url's word list included 'item'/'record', which commonly name public no-ownership resources
findings.summary: The path-keyword list (user|account|invoice|order|profile|record|item|document|report) treated any small numeric ID after 'item' or 'record' as an IDOR risk, but these two words just as often name a PUBLIC catalog resource with no ownership concept at all -- an e-commerce product page at /item/42 has no 'owner' to enumerate away from, so flagging it as an IDOR risk is a category error, not a security finding, on completely ordinary browsing URLs.
findings.fix: Removed 'item' and 'record' from the keyword list, keeping the words (user/account/invoice/order/profile) that reliably name a user-scoped resource in normal usage.

findings.title: Three page-checks SRI/sandbox checks repeated the already-fixed 'fires on every ordinary third-party embed' pattern from scanner-07
findings.summary: page-script-missing-sri (medium) and page-third-party-script-unconstrained-by-csp (high) fire on any third-party script without SRI regardless of vendor, including Google Analytics/GTM/ads/payment SDKs that cannot practically use SRI because they are continuously updated by the vendor -- the identical false-positive class already found and downgraded for the legacy sri-missing check in headers.json (AUDIT-008 scanner-07), just not yet applied to the newer PageCheck-architecture equivalents in my scope. page-third-party-iframe-no-sandbox (medium) has the same relationship to the already-downgraded iframe-third-party-without-sandbox: it fires on routine legitimate embeds (video players, maps, payment widgets, chat widgets) that omit sandbox because it breaks required functionality.
findings.fix: Downgraded page-script-missing-sri medium->low, page-third-party-script-unconstrained-by-csp high->medium, and page-third-party-iframe-no-sandbox medium->low, matching the severities scanner-07 already established for the equivalent legacy checks; added a sentence to each riskImpact noting how common the flagged configuration is on legitimate sites.

findings.title: ~15 more api.json entries typed 'header' despite their detectors reading only body/URL, understating regex-guess uncertainty
findings.summary: Beyond the mass-assignment and graphql-introspection entries (scanner-16/18), soap-endpoint, xml-rpc, api-graphql-batch-queries, api-graphql-error-stack-trace, api-openapi-default-values-sensitive, api-openapi-server-url-leak, and api-jwt-hs256-weak-secret are pure body regexes with zero header interaction but were typed 'header' (93% confidence); api-graphql-suggestions-enabled, api-graphql-error-stack-trace, api-openapi-security-scheme-weak, api-jsonp-callback, api-soap-wsdl-publicly-accessible, and api-websocket-no-origin-validation read both url and body (no header at all) but were also typed 'header'; api-bearer-header-leak reads only the URL string.
findings.fix: Corrected each to 'body-pattern' (70% confidence), 'combined' (85%), or 'url-check' (82%) matching what the paired detector in api.ts actually inspects.

findings.title: api-rate-limit-per-ip-no-auth read an unrelated response header as evidence and overclaimed 'no authentication required'
findings.summary: One firing branch treated a response carrying x-forwarded-for (a client-IP-forwarding header, rarely present on a response at all) as evidence that rate limiting is 'keyed only on client IP' -- the two facts are unrelated. Separately, the evidence text asserted 'no authentication required' from the scanner's own request lacking an Authorization header, which is true of nearly every passive scan regardless of whether the endpoint actually requires auth; a properly protected endpoint returning 401 with rate-limit headers attached would look identical to this detector.
findings.fix: Removed the x-forwarded-for branch (kept only the x-ratelimit-limit signal) and reworded evidence to prompt verification of the auth requirement rather than assert its absence. Also softened api-rate-limit-headers-not-enforced-on-paths's evidence, which asserted a X-RateLimit-Remaining absence means the 'cap not enforced' as fact when a server may only emit that header near the limit.

findings.title: api-graphql-error-stack-trace's bare stacktrace-key match claimed GraphQL context it never verified
findings.summary: One branch fired on any "stacktrace":" appearing anywhere in a response body with no requirement the response came from a GraphQL endpoint or carried a GraphQL error envelope, yet the evidence unconditionally states 'GraphQL error.extensions.stacktrace leaked' -- a stack trace leaking from a non-GraphQL API (a real bug, but a different check's concern) would be mislabeled.
findings.fix: Added a GraphQL-context gate (/graphql URL or a JSON 'extensions' object present, which is where the GraphQL spec places error extension data) before either stacktrace pattern is evaluated.

findings.title: api.ts and supply-chain.ts detectors never excluded doc/tutorial <pre>/<code> blocks, unlike vibe-code.ts's already-fixed equivalent
findings.summary: None of api.ts's body-regex detectors (soap-endpoint, xml-rpc, api-jwt-hs256-weak-secret's jwt.sign(...) pattern, etc.) or supply-chain.ts's config-file fingerprint detectors (lockfile/requirements/Gemfile/composer/Dockerfile/.env) excluded <pre>/<code>/<kbd>/<samp> regions before matching, the same gap already fixed for vibe-code.ts (AUDIT-008 vibe-01) because this product's own /docs pages, and any tutorial/blog post, render example payloads and config snippets as literal text in those tags.
findings.fix: Wrapped every detector in both files with stripDocBlocks() at export time, mirroring vibe-code.ts's existing wrapper pattern exactly. No effect on the primary detection case (a raw exposed file/API response has no HTML tags to strip).
